people.label: Luis D. Elizondo

people.narrative: Elizondo is the hinge on which the 2017 break turns. timeline.label: TTSA announces metamaterials acquisition
timeline.text: The ADAM Research Project announces possession of material reportedly from an advanced aerospace vehicle of unknown origin; Steve Justice says its structure and composition match no known military or commercial application.

timeline.label: DD Form 1910 released via FOIA
timeline.text: The unredacted form is published, identifying Elizondo by name and OUSD(I) title as the officer who cleared the three video files in August 2017.

timeline.label: Navy designates the objects UAP
timeline.text: Joseph Gradisher: 'The Navy designates the objects contained in these videos as unidentified aerial phenomena' — while stating the Navy never released them and that no DOPSR record of an unrestricted-release request exists.

timeline.label: TTSA-Army CRADA signed
timeline.text: Jeffery Langhout for the Army GVSC and Kari DeLonge for TTSA sign a five-year cooperative research agreement covering inertial mass reduction, metamaterials, quantum communications, beamed energy propulsion and active camouflage.

timeline.label: CRADA announced publicly
timeline.text: Dr. Joseph Cannon of Army Futures Command calls TTSA 'an exciting, non-traditional source for novel materials'. The Army releases the agreement text the next day.

timeline.label: Gough reverses: 'Neither AATIP nor AAWSAP were UAP related'
timeline.text: The Department repudiates its own May 2019 acknowledgement, saying Sherwood was repeating an earlier spokesperson who 'is no longer with my organization', and that AATIP 'did not pursue research and investigation into unidentified aerial phenomena'.

timeline.label: Army withholds all CRADA correspondence
timeline.text: CCDC FOIA Officer Joy L. Linton locates 29 emails totalling 100 pages of TTSA-Army correspondence and denies all of them under exemptions (b)(4) and (b)(5).

timeline.label: DoD authorises release of the three videos
timeline.text: The Department releases FLIR1, Gimbal and GoFast officially, calls their earlier appearance the product of 'unauthorized releases in 2007 and 2017', and states the phenomena 'remain characterized as unidentified'.

timeline.label: 'The truth... is that I ran the program'
timeline.text: Elizondo writes to Susan Gough noting she corrected the AATIP/UAP statement but never the statement about him. The letter sits in the Department's own FOIA reading room.

timeline.label: Elizondo, Mellon and Justice leave TTSA
timeline.text: The three government-side principals depart; the aerospace and materials work winds down and the entity later renames itself To The Stars Inc.

timeline.label: Elizondo files DoD IG complaint
timeline.text: Alleging 'malicious activities, coordinated disinformation, professional misconduct, whistleblower reprisal and explicit threats', naming Garry Reid, Susan Gough and Neill Tipton.

timeline.label: 60 Minutes segment
timeline.text: Elizondo, Mellon and Navy aviators appear in a CBS 60 Minutes report on UAP in restricted U.S. airspace, weeks before the ODNI preliminary assessment.

timeline.label: Gough's partial re-reversal
timeline.text: The Department concedes the AATIP contract 'allowed for research drawn from a wide variety of sources, including reports of UAPs' while insisting UAP examination 'was not the purpose of AATIP'. The denial of Elizondo's role does not move.

timeline.label: Garry Reid removed
timeline.text: Reid is removed as Director for Defense Intelligence after DoD IG investigations substantiate ethics violations, 65 instances of official business on personal email, and unwelcome physical contact with subordinates.

timeline.label: FOIA 18-F-0324 released
timeline.text: Four years and eight months after the request, DoD releases the two resignation letters and the two Garry Reid memoranda — eight pages.

timeline.label: DoD IG interviews Elizondo
timeline.text: A 103-page transcript of the Inspector General's interview of Elizondo is later released under FOIA, along with 126 pages of DoD IG UAP emails in February 2024.

timeline.label: AARO Historical Record Volume 1
timeline.text: AARO's report treats 2009 as the standup year for AAWSAP and AATIP and states it found 'no evidence for the USG reverse-engineering narrative provided by interviewees'.

timeline.label: Imminent published after a year of DOPSR review
timeline.text: Elizondo's memoir debuts at number one on the New York Times bestseller list. He later testifies that 'what is in the book is what I was told I am allowed to talk about'.

timeline.label: Sworn testimony before House Oversight
timeline.text: Elizondo answers 'Yes' under oath to secret UAP crash retrieval programs and to their reverse-engineering purpose, and describes 'a culture of suppression and intimidation that I have personally been victim to'.

timeline.label: Luna task force holds its first UAP hearing
timeline.text: 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection' — the House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets takes testimony from Nuccetelli, Borland, Wiggins, Knapp and POGO's Joe Spielberger.

timeline.label: Luna demands 46 UAP video files from the Department of War
timeline.text: Chairwoman Anna Paulina Luna writes to Secretary Pete Hegseth demanding 46 UAP video files with an April 14 deadline, finding AARO's responses 'less than adequate'. The FLIR1/Gimbal/GoFast release chain of 2017-2020 is the precedent she is invoking.

timeline.label: UAP Science Advisory Council formed
timeline.text: ODNI, AARO and the White House ask Avi Loeb to assemble a 14-member scientific council to advise on resolving the nature of UAP and support a new interagency UAP Governance Board. Tim Gallaudet, who testified alongside Elizondo in 2024, is a member.

timeline.label: Reckoning scheduled for publication
timeline.text: Elizondo's second book, promising 'previously undisclosed evidence', is scheduled for HarperCollins release with a 20-date speaking tour. Its DOPSR status is not yet public.

aatip.desc: The Department of Defense's public position on AATIP in strict chronological order, which is the single most useful artifact this domain produces. (1) 16 December 2017, Thomas Crosson: the program existed and was shut down in 2012 because 'there were other, higher priority issues that merit' the funding. (2) 22 May 2019, Christopher Sherwood: AATIP 'did pursue research and investigation into unidentified aerial phenomena'. (3) 1 June 2019, Sherwood: 'Mr. Elizondo had no responsibilities with regard to the AATIP program while he worked in OUSDI, up until the time he resigned effective 10/4/2017.' (4) 13 June 2019, Susan Gough: the authenticated Reid memo 'makes no change to previous statements. Mr. Elizondo had no assigned responsibilities for AATIP while he was in OUSD(I)'; DIA administered AATIP and Elizondo was never assigned to DIA. (5) 6 December 2019, Gough: 'Neither AATIP nor AAWSAP were UAP related'; Sherwood's May statement was accurately reported but 'not entirely fact-based' because he was repeating a previous spokesperson who 'is no longer with my organization'. (6) 21 May 2021, Gough: the contract 'allowed for research drawn from a wide variety of sources, including reports of UAPs. However, the examination of UAP observations was not the purpose of AATIP.' (7) 8 March 2024, AARO Historical Record Report Volume 1: 2009 is the standup year for AAWSAP and AATIP, and 'none of the programs mentioned by interviewees are UAP reverse-engineering programs.' Across seven years the position on whether AATIP touched UAP moved twice; the position on whether Elizondo had a role in it never moved at all.

gaps: The outcome of Elizondo's May 2021 DoD Inspector General complaint has never been published. FOIA releases have produced the IG's February 2023 interview transcript of Elizondo (103 pages), 126 pages of IG emails released February 2024, and 40 further pages in March 2025 — but no finding, no substantiation determination, and no corrective action. The DoD IG report released publicly on 7 January 2026 (case DODOIG-2025-000932, closed February 2025, not substantiated) concerns a different, heavily redacted complainant whose profile matches David Grusch, not Elizondo. Do not conflate them.

The attachments to Elizondo's 5 June 2019 letter to DoD Public Affairs — the documents he says substantiate his AATIP role — were withheld from the FOIA release. They are the single highest-value unreleased item in this domain.

The identity of the 'Defense Department official' who handed Christopher Mellon the three video files in the Pentagon parking lot is unknown. Mellon has never named the person and says he retains the original packaging.

No technical output from the TTSA ADAM Research Project has ever been published — not by EarthTech International, not by TTSA, and not by the U.S. Army under the CRADA. The 29 emails / 100 pages of Army-TTSA correspondence remain withheld in full under FOIA exemptions (b)(4) and (b)(5) as of the last public accounting. No appeal outcome has been located.

The provenance of the ADAM specimens is undocumented. TTSA's SEC materials say some have been in 'documented possession since the mid-1990s' without naming the chain of custody, the acquiring party, or the recovery event.

The Department has never reconciled two facts in its own files: that Elizondo allegedly had no assigned AATIP responsibilities, and that in August 2017 he was the officer who submitted the DD Form 1910 clearing the AATIP-associated video files, while in September 2017 he drafted a memorandum helping Neill Tipton assume 'the new responsibilities for AATIP'. No official has ever been asked this on the record under oath.

The claim that Pentagon spokeswoman Dana White confirmed in December 2017 that Elizondo led AATIP is widely repeated but no primary transcript, press release or contemporaneous quotation has been located. The documented 2017 confirmation, sourced to Elizondo's own FOIA-released letter, is only that a DoD Press Secretary verified he was an OUSD(I) staff member.

The full AFOSI file on the 2017-2018 inquiry into Elizondo's handling of the video material has not been released. The Reid memoranda record that the inquiry occurred and closed with a finding that the videos were unclassified, but the underlying investigative record is unlocated.

TTSA's total capital raised across both Regulation A offerings and its final disposition of the aerospace and science assets are not established. The 2018 Form 1-K and the 2018 semiannual filing are public; the wind-down of the Aerospace Division after the December 2020 departures is documented only in press reporting.

Whether Reckoning (27 August 2026) was submitted to DOPSR, and whether anything was struck, is unknown as of 12 August 2026. Given that Imminent's year-long DOPSR review is Elizondo's strongest single credibility argument, the review status of the second book is a priority research item.

Susan Gough's exact departure date from the DoD UAP spokesperson role, and the identity of her successor, are not established here. The Department was renamed the Department of War in 2025 and its public affairs structure for UAP matters after that point needs mapping.

The 'previous spokesperson' Gough said was 'no longer with my organization' — the person whose 2017 information Sherwood was allegedly repeating — has never been named. Identifying that individual would establish whether the Department's original 2017 position was itself sourced to someone with direct knowledge.
